articles.headline: The Outlast Trials Is An Exercise In Bad Taste And Good Politics
keyFacts: The Outlast Trials is a multiplayer survival horror prequel where players undergo mental conditioning and deadly tests within the Murkoff Corporation during the Cold War.
The author stated that the game features extreme graphic violence and places players in horrific scenarios designed to test their compatibility for government-backed sleeper cell programs.
The game's narrative ties into alternative history and political violence, illustrating how manufactured military supersoldier programs ultimately turn their violence back home.
body: In Rex Millerâs 1987 horror novel Slob, Chicago is under the blight of “Chaingang,” a 500-pound killer whose hunger for food and flesh is unequaled. Despite his appearance and more odorous stench, the walking death manages to maneuver with little detection due to what’s described as an uncanny charisma. He is effectively camouflaged. Such an unusual make of man, it turns out, is not born. Chaingang was designed by the Pentagon, part of a covert project to create an unstoppable murder machine to turn the tide in Vietnam. A Michael Myers for Uncle Sam.
Then he came home. They always do.

The Outlast Trials is entirely consumed by this boomerang paradigm. In the co-op game, you and other lower rungs of society are subjected to mental conditioning tests. Solve puzzles, elude enemy detection and, occasionally, murder in unthinkable ways. A multiplayer prequel to Red Barrelâs hit 2013 survival horror OutlastÂ in which a citizen journalist discovers a creepy mental asylum providing cover for a backfiring supersoldier program, Trials is set in the late â50s, an era defined by Cold War paranoia. The game is set in the bowels of The Murkoff Corporation, a research firm tasked with creating sleeper cells.

With seemingly no limit on financing or bodies, the company is pushing the outer limits of narcotics and mind control. An elevated MK Ultra, Murkoff isn’t just designing the drugs a Charles Manson type might trip on; it’s drafting blueprints for its own BTK. Along with two or three friends, your compatibility will be tested in controlled environments, slaughterhouses recreating places of commerce, faith, bread and circuses. You will be asked to commit horrors. If you abstain, those horrors will be committed on you.

Recommended to me by author Grady Hendrix, Slob was published in the late â80s but soaked in the remnants of â60s counterculture, a lurid paperback made layered by its government paranoia. Tales of supersoldier programs are not unique. Half of all genre fiction seems to be about them and about half of those posit these programs as a bad thing. What makes it more interesting is that it has the clarity to paint the bigger picture, the fortitude to name the national projects that such mad science benefits, on whose behalf, and at what cost. It’s those key similarities that made me feel like Trials is influenced by Millerâs admittedly obscure work, and that make me far more confident the game took beats from the more popular, non-fiction 2019 tome Chaos by Tom O’Neill with Dan Piepenbring, which attempts to chronicle how many of these programs were real all along.

There is not a subtle bone in The Outlast Trials’ body. Each environment is saturated with blood. Where the heaps of mannequin parts end and the mountains of eviscerated limbs begin is indistinguishable. It is, quite possibly, the gnarliest game ever made, a truly inspired feat in an experience that may lead to heated debates over which “execution” is the most depraved. Due to their pacing and agonizing presentation, tarring, feathering and castrating a man dressed like Donald Duck can be as stomach-turning as pulverizing a judgeâs ankle bones with gavels. One trial implies that you, yes you, created the AIDS virus.

As you complete each trial, you must outmaneuver previous failed experiments whose augmentations, disfigurements, and madness make them incompatible with field work. Youâre also being pursued by the “prime assets,” singular all-star murderers whose reputation and charisma caught the attention of the Murkoff Corporation. This includes an oedipal Miami gangster, a leather cop with a lightning fetish, and conjoined twins who, despite their impossible disfigurements, converse like guests on William F. Buckleyâs Firing Line. Theyâre the Village People from hell. They are not just your enemies. They are enemies of life. Of dignity. Civil rights. Labor movements. Democracy. They are totems of empire enlisted on behalf of Murkoff, who are working on behalf of western interests.

In one of the gameâs endings, you awaken in the Congo at the far end of a firing line, sitting on your knees. Your interrogators demand to know the significance of a string of words, unknowingly speaking out your trigger phase. When you come to a second time, bodies have piled up and your thumbs are submerged in a manâs eye sockets.Â Previous endings follow a similar structure. You awaken in a Cuban hotel room, caked in blood. You come to in China, having freshly produced sexual blackmail. In the Saigon ending, youâre behind the wheel of a car, barreling past a checkpoint with a bomb strapped to your chest, mirroring real embassy bombings throughout the early ’50s. How this prequel will ultimately tie in with the incidents at Mount Massive Asylum feels less significant than how it will tie in with a larger alternative history. If Iâm allowed to trust my gut, I can think of one especially prominent political assassination that the game might be building up to.

This doesnât make the connective tissue to the other Outlasts insignificant, but the greater weight is less on the details than the inevitable arc. The Outlast Trials is about a weapons factory. Vampires and werewolves made on assembly lines and shipped overseas to violate political movements the powers that be deem inconvenient. To uphold American might. But inevitably, the violence returns. It returns to Mount Massive. It returns in lost boys and biker gangs. In summers of serial killers. In political assassinations carried out by individuals with holistically unplaceable values. It comes from an indifference to life, echoed from the top, festering all the way down. From the promise of stability being replaced with casino games. It is honed violence, intentionally manufactured for one purpose, but spilling over into oneâs backyard. It is a political project, but one that can only imagine itself on one end of the knife. And once it’s loose, look out behind you.

articles.headline: How Trump and his allies seek to interfere the US midterm elections
keyFacts: Donald Trump and his administration are attempting to interfere with US midterm elections by filing lawsuits and seeking voter roll data.
The Justice Department sued Alaska to block election certification and sued California to force officials to sequester thousands of ballots.
Legal experts said the administration's efforts are legally weak and unlikely to succeed, though they could cause post-election delays.
body: Donald Trump is waging a brazen effort to interfere with voting in this year’s midterm elections, escalating concerns that the federal government will try to slow down certification of election results – a strategy that could create chaos when the new Congress is seated next year.

Experts are certain the administration’s efforts to subvert America’s elections will not work. And some have bemoaned “fearmongering” about far-fetched scenarios that are unlikely to go anywhere in court.
But after the attack on the Capitol on January 6, 2021, voting lawyers and other democracy groups aren’t dismissing the possibility of anything.
The potential for interference is related to how close the contest winds up being, said Ned Foley, a professor at the Ohio State University and an expert on disputed elections.
“The more it looks like a blowout or a ‘blue tsunami’, the harder it’s going to be for any attempt to make mischief to get any traction,” he said.

“I put the probability of these impactful nightmare scenarios materializing at under 50%, so I’m not expecting them to make a difference,” he added. But, he said there are “risks of weird things happening, and you need to pay attention to them even if the risk is rather low”.

The Trump administration’s efforts to interfere began last year with an effort to collect detailed voter roll information from nearly every state. And it has continued into the final days of the election, in which the government has sought to sequester ballots in California and filed a legally thin lawsuit to try to stop the certification of election results in Alaska, where there is a hotly contested US Senate race.
The US constitution gives the states, not the federal government, authority to run elections. And it gives the president no power when it comes to voting.

“The type of conduct we have seen from the administration right now is unlike anything we have ever seen as far as federal attempts to interfere with the elections,” said Danielle Lang, a voting rights attorney at the Campaign Legal Center, a watchdog group. “It’s amounting to relatively little because the federal government is just not in charge of the levers of election administration and it can’t force itself to be involved in those levers of election administration.”
Here are some of the main ways Trump and his allies have sought to interfere with the election process – or could.
Using emergency power

Some of Trump’s allies on the right have encouraged him to invoke emergency powers to exert influence over elections, including potentially seizing voting equipment and sending troops to the polls. Trump has refused to rule out such ideas.
The move would be illegal – the president has no power, emergency or otherwise, over elections. Courts would likely quickly step in and stop such efforts.
But even if courts do step in to prevent things like ballot seizures, it could still cause chaos, confusion, and delay in a post-election period where there is uncertainty about the election results.
Stopping certification

The Trump administration’s most aggressive judicial effort to interfere in the election so far has come in Alaska, where it has taken the extraordinary step of asking a federal court to step in before election day and block certification if the Republican candidate loses.

Alaska has an extremely competitive US senate race this year between Republican Dan S Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, and the outcome could determine which party controls the chamber. In a complicated twist, there is also a Dan J Sullivan on the ballot. The Alaska supreme court allowed Dan J Sullivan to stay on the ballot earlier this year in response to a ruling from the Alaska division of elections disqualifying him.

On 23 October, the justice department sued Alaska and asked a judge to block certification “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”. It’s unclear how such an investigation would take place after an election, since U.S. voters cast their ballots secretly. Trump said he ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit.

The saga got more complicated days later when the New York Times reported that operatives aligned with Peltola were behind the effort to get Dan J Sullivan on the ballot as part of an effort to siphon votes away from the Republican candidate. Democrats had denied being behind the effort. Trump reacted angrily to the report. “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot,” he wrote on Truth Social.

The justice department’s legal argument for stopping certification is also extremely thin. In its lawsuit, the justice department pointed to broad language in the preamble to the 1993 National Voter Registration Act that says one of the purposes of the law is to “protect the integrity of the electoral process”. Election experts have said it is not possible to hang a legal case on such vague language.
The justice department knows it is going to lose the Alaska lawsuit, but may have another goal in mind, Richard Pildes, an election law scholar at New York University, wrote in a blog post.

“Even if DOJ loses in the federal courts, as it will, the litigation will give ammunition to anyone in the certification process, particularly the Lt. Gov., who might seek to delay or deny certification to the Democrat, Mary Peltola, if she wins, based on the claim that voters who voted for Daniel J. Sullivan (and perhaps ranked no other candidate) meant to vote for in the incumbent Republican Senator, Daniel S. Sullivan,” he wrote. In Alaska, the governor and Lt. Gov sign the certificate for the winning candidate that is sent to the US Senate.
Noncitizen voting

A key element of the Trump administration’s efforts to interfere in the election is a push to create the false impression that there are large numbers of noncitizens on the rolls who are voting – and perhaps to use that argument to mount post-election legal challenges. Studies have shown that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare and that when it does occur, it is because of confusion.

The administration’s push to find noncitizen voters began last year, when the justice department filed lawsuits across the country seeking to have states turn over their voter rolls – each state is in charge of its own list of registered voters and there is no single federal voter database in the United States. In an extraordinary rebuke, more than two dozen different federal judges – including some appointed by Trump – rejected the requests from the government, saying they were unlawful.

Unable to get voter lists directly from the states, the Department of Homeland Security obtained public voter roll information and began running it against its own records to hunt for noncitizens. It has not been transparent about its methodology, and many experts have been skeptical of its accuracy.

On 13 October, the justice department delivered a USB drive with a password written on a Post-it note to election officials in Los Angeles county purporting to contain the names of 20,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls (there are more than 23 million registered voters in California). It gave the state 48 hours to review the names and sequester ballots cast by anyone whose citizenship had not been confirmed.

The state refused, citing concerns about cybersecurity and the administration’s methodology. On 15 October, the justice department sued California, asking a judge to order the state to sequester the ballots. As the justice department pushed the claims, they also announced the arrest of 28 noncitizens who allegedly had voted at one point in the state. US district judge David O Carter ruled against the justice department on Wednesday. The government is appealing that decision.

On 26 October, the justice department made a similar demand in Washington state, asking election officials to investigate the citizenship of 400 voters and sequester ballots for those whose citizenship it could not confirm.
The justice department has also threatened to prosecute election officials who process ballots from noncitizens.

Despite the aggressive approach from the justice department, there’s reason to be skeptical of their list in California. When local election officials sampled 200 names from the list they provided, they found many of them had already been canceled. Election officials also said a “high percentage” of those flagged appeared to be born in the United States. Washington secretary of state Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, responded to the justice department on Wednesday, saying it believed the list the government provided was inaccurate.
While the justice department’s efforts to get ballots segregated before the election are unlikely to succeed, they could offer a pretext for a post-election effort to challenge the results.

“There will be an argument – I can almost guarantee it – that a bunch of ballots in California should be thrown out because they didn’t segregate them,” said Ben Berwick, an election lawyer at Protect Democracy, a nonprofit that works on democracy issues. “I think this will be laughed out of court if they try to bring this past post-election.”
“That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be worried or we don’t need to prepare for it,” he added.

Justin Levitt, a former justice department and White House official who worked on voting rights issues, said the government’s case was so weak it would have little chance of succeeding before or after election day. The administration’s lawsuits, he said, are best understood as press releases masquerading as legal complaints.

“There’s no part of the administration’s file that is designed to operate in a fashion where a court will make any meaningful ruling,” said Levitt, who is a professor at Loyola law school in Los Angeles. “There are ways in which the law works where a good claim today that cannot be brought just because it’s too early becomes a viable claim tomorrow. But time does not transmogrify crap into gold.”
Efforts to delay certification at the local and state level

After the 2020 election, Trump and allies put pressure on little-known officials at the local and state level to try and halt the certification of election winners. None of that worked, but election deniers have gained a foothold on local election boards throughout the country – positions from which they could try and slow down the certification process.

Election lawyers are well prepared for this possibility and are confident that judges would quickly end such efforts and order officials to certify the valid winners of elections. In the past, courts have stepped in to force election officials to certify.

“Ultimately, you cannot pull a contested election out of thin air, and there are processes here and you can’t just manufacture contests where they aren’t real,” Lang said. “I don’t imagine it looking all that different than it has in past election cycles where we’ve seen some issues with certification that ultimately come to a resolution. We’ve had counties that don’t want to certify; we’ve dealt with that before.”
Shenanigans on 3 January 2027

Efforts to delay or halt certification could be aimed at 3 January 2027, the date when the new Congress convenes. There’s concern that the Trump administration could use its various legal and rhetorical challenges to the results as a basis to try and block new members from being seated. The US constitution says: “Each House shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members,” giving both the US House and Senate leeway to handle disputed elections.

Federal law requires the governor and secretary of state to sign a certificate certifying a senator-elect’s win and send it to the Senate. In the past, when there has been a post-election dispute about the winner of a Senate race, the candidate who has the certificate gets seated provisionally while the Senate rules committee investigates. In cases where the margin of the race is close and there is no certificate, no senator has gotten seated until the dispute is resolved at the state level. After the 2008 elections, for example, a US Senate seat from Minnesota remained vacant for months while Norm Coleman and Al Franken battled in a close recount for months (Democrat Franken was eventually certified the winner).

“We’ve had disputes over Senate elections, like Coleman versus Franken in Minnesota in 2008, but they never determined which party is the majority,” Foley said. “If partisan control over the Senate hinges on something like Coleman verses Franken, it will be a politically consequential and fraught moment as the dispute remains unsettled. It also depends on how irresponsible the rhetoric is around the dispute.”

There have been lengthy post-election disputes over US Senate seats before. Pildes, the NYU election expert, suggested that the justice department’s efforts to interfere in Alaska may be aimed at bringing such a long-shot challenge in the US Senate.
Trump himself has suggested that Republicans refuse to seat Peltola if she wins.

“You’re going to have to see what happens. It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don’t know how you could allow somebody like that to run. It’s so unfair when you look at that,” Trump said on Thursday.
In the US House, there is also the possibility of maneuvering, though it is more complicated.

Unlike the Senate, the House is not a continuing body and ceases to exist at noon on 3 January. That means that any challenge to a member-elect would be heard by the new House – one where Democrats are expected to have a majority.

There’s worry about another longshot strategy. A single bureaucratic official, the clerk of the House, is responsible for putting together the roll of new members. There’s some speculation that Mike Johnson, acting under pressure from Trump, could fire the current clerk of the House and replace him with a loyalist willing to exclude some Democratic members-elect from the roll. Republicans could then theoretically move to hold a speaker vote and try and maintain their majority without the seated Democrats – a strategy that would require the support of the other Republicans in the House.
Democrats would assuredly go to federal court to stop such an effort.

Many scholars are skeptical it would work. Derek T Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, has described the speculation about replacing the clerk of the House as “sophisticated disaster porn”. Johnson has also pledged to seat Democrats who win.

“It strikes me as quite unlikely, to me, at least, that this group of Republicans–the one that takes days to choose a speaker and that regularly cannot maintain order in its ranks–is going to have the cohesion and coordination to pull off this kind of activity, which, to emphasize, can be thwarted by other means, either politically or judicially,” he wrote earlier this year.
But Brian C Kalt, a professor at Michigan State University who has written about contested house elections, said: “I think it’s very hard after January 6th to just write off concerns like this.

“It’s reasonable for people to study the issue, think about the issue, worry about the issue. But I don’t think that it’s some imminent threat,” he added. “If there are going to be any shenanigans, there will be initial steps, signs that will be available. This isn’t just something they can spring.”
Interference at the polls

The Trump administration has refused to rule out the possibility of immigration agents being at the polls, a move that would violate federal law. Speaking in September, DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin refused to categorically rule it out. DHS agents were also canvassing houses earlier this year, inquiring about people’s citizenship and whether they had voted. (A federal court blocked the government from continuing to do this in October). Federal law prohibits armed troops from being at the polls.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be,” he said. Asked about the possibility of ICE agents at the polls, Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the justice department’s civil rights division, told 60 Minutes recently that “there is no plan to do that.” The justice department, which plans to conduct a significant poll-monitoring operation on election day, has also said it will not use ICE or FBI agents as poll monitors.

Still, election officials are planning on what to do if immigration officers do show up at the polls and there are several lawsuits seeking to block them from being deployed. Democrats are also planning on sending their own monitors to the polls to ensure voters aren’t intimidated or interfered with.
Ballot seizures

One of the Trump administration’s most aggressive efforts to intervene in elections came in January, when FBI agents descended on an election warehouse in Fulton county, Georgia, and seized all ballots from the 2020 presidential election.

Trump lost Georgia in 2020 by 11,779 votes – a result that was confirmed by both recounts and audits. Trump has been obsessed with overturning the result ever since the election and he and allies have pushed several conspiracy theories since 2020 to argue that he didn’t lose. Those theories have all been debunked, which is why it was stunning that a federal magistrate judge signed off on a warrant to seize the ballots in January based on the same theories. (As is customary, the judge did not give a reason for why she felt there was enough probable cause).

Now, there is concern that the Trump administration could try a similar approach elsewhere and convince sympathetic judges to approve warrants to seize ballots. Such an effort could be done with an eye towards making it harder for election results to be certified at the local and state level, Berwick said.

“There’s a big leap between what happened in Fulton county, which was a magistrate being willing to sign a warrant for materials that were over five years old, and a magistrate being willing to sign a warrant for live ballot materials,” Lang said. “Everybody is preparing for every worst-case scenario, but I am very hopeful that we are unlikely to see a warrant signed for live materials.”

articles.headline: Obama had the Tea Party. Trump has ‘No Kings.’ You know how this story ends
keyFacts: President Donald Trump faced opposition similar to the Tea Party under Barack Obama, resulting in the formation of the progressive 'No Kings' movement.
The author stated that the No Kings movement is expected to help Democrats win back both the House and the Senate in November.
The author noted that Senator John Fetterman might join the GOP if Democrats flip just four Senate seats, potentially allowing Republicans to keep control.
body: In January 2009, then-President Barack Obama had no sooner assumed office after handily defeating the Republican nominee, John McCain , when opposition to his overreaching agenda galvanized a center-right movement. At the suggestion of CNBC editor Rick Santelli, whose live, on-air rant of Feb. 19 of that year perfectly captured the spirit of the opposition, the modern-day Tea Party was formed.

Initially, the Tea Party was ridiculed by Democrats and ignored by the media — despite its large, nationwide Tax Day Tea Parties. It wasn’t until GOP and Tea Party-endorsed candidate Scott Brown won Ted Kennedy’s former U.S. Senate seat in a special election held Jan. 19, 2010, in liberal Massachusetts, that anyone really started taking the Tea Party seriously.

Turning the page to 2025, one notices a comparable situation. President Donald Trump , who fell short of a 50% majority in a basically two-person race against Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, defeating her by 49.91% to 48.43% in the popular vote, assumed the office of the presidency falsely claiming to have won it in a landslide.
BELTWAY CONFIDENTIAL — OBAMA IS ‘TIRED OF BEING DIVIDED’: POT, MEET KETTLE

From there, his overreaching agenda and far too numerous and outlandish executive orders led to the birth of the progressive “ No Kings ” movement — which was quickly dismissed by Trump and the GOP despite its initial, massive, nationwide rallies. But it wasn’t until Democrats started to win a disproportionate share of special elections nationwide, even in red states like Florida, that the No Kings movement also gained respect.

And the parallels between the Tea Party and No Kings movements don’t end there — far outweighing their differences. Both claimed to be mostly volunteer, leaderless, decentralized movements committed to nonviolence. Though Santelli called for the Tea Party’s formation, he refused to lead it. And just like the Tea Party, No Kings has state, regional, and local leaders who help organize mass rallies.

To boot, the Tea Party had help from established national groups including FreedomWorks and Club for Growth, while No Kings is supported by MoveOn, Third Act, and the American Civil Liberties Union. Both announced clear-cut agendas that, oddly enough, shared opposition to overreaching executive power — whether it be from Obama or Trump. And a quick look at the respective presidential job approval numbers of both men — Obama in October 2010 and Trump in October 2026 — reveals both were underwater.

No doubt, the Tea Party’s greatest impact occurred during the 2010 midterm elections when it reached the peak of its political influence. It helped flip 63 House seats, six Senate seats, six governorships, and a record-breaking 680 state legislative seats. It might have flipped two additional Senate seats had more moderate candidates prevailed in the Delaware and Nevada GOP primaries. But even had they flipped those seats, Democrats would have kept control of the Senate by a 51-49 margin.

All of this sounds eerily familiar. The No Kings movement, too, went a bit adrift in two key Democratic Senate 2026 primary battles held in Maine and Michigan, as well as some congressional primaries around the country — nominating socialists and controversial candidates when their more moderate and experienced counterparts would probably have had an easier, less costly path to victory.
OPINION: VOTE LIKE AMERICA’S FUTURE IS ON THE BALLOT. BECAUSE IT IS

While this may keep the number of flipped seats lower than the Tea Party midterm elections of 2010, it seems more likely than not that the No Kings movement will help Democrats win back both the House and Senate come November.

But there is a major caveat. Keep your eyes on Sen. John Fetterman (D-PA). If the Democrats flip just four Senate seats, there are glaring signs Fetterman may join the GOP, enabling Republicans to maintain control of the upper chamber. However, given the current climate, it appears the Democrats will flip at least five seats to win Senate control. And, if so, the No Kings movement will have matched, or even surpassed, the Tea Party’s 2010 success.

Don Adams is a founder of the tri-state region (Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware) Independence Hall Tea Party (2009-2014) and former president of its political action committee. He has worked on numerous Republican political campaigns and public affairs projects.

articles.headline: I took two iPhones on vacation. The Duo won me over.
keyFacts: A tech reporter tested Apple's new iPhone Duo on a five-day vacation, using it alongside an iPhone 17 Pro Max as a safety net.
The reporter experienced frustrations with broken apps, missing Face ID, and a weaker camera system, but ultimately grew to like the device.
The Duo proved durable through multiple accidental drops and stands out as a mainstream, highly polished foldable device within Apple's ecosystem.
body: “I think I’m going to switch back to my other iPhone.”

I’ll admit, I said this multiple times during my five-day vacation with the new iPhone Duo, after encountering frustrations with broken apps, unfamiliar gestures (a return to Touch ID, argh!), and camera concerns that had me lugging around two phones.
By the time the trip was over, I didn’t want to go back.

When I first unboxed the Duo, a loaner from Apple, I was genuinely intrigued. I felt a flutter of anticipation as I peeled back the factory seal wrap and booted up the device. In retrospect, this was probably the first signal that Duo was going to ultimately win me over.

As a tech reporter, I’ve received a lot of test devices over the years, so unfortunately, opening a package with a new gadget inside is no longer the thrill it used to be. But sometime in the days leading up to the Duo’s ship date, I found myself actually wanting one – I had started doing the math and comparing upgrade options that would allow me to afford the $2K the phone would cost. I started scrolling TikTok reviews of Duo cases. I hesitated not only because of the price but because moving to the Duo is a major change – especially coming from an iPhone 17 Pro Max. The phones could not be more different.

As I was about to head out on vacation when the Duo arrived, I decided to tote my 17 Pro Max with me too, as something of a safety net. I ended up using the Duo more, and grew comfortable with it over the course of the trip, despite some frustrations.

There’s always a psychological switching cost in changing phones, but particularly going from a high-end phone to a more experimental device like the Duo. For someone used to the iPhone’s long-perfected tech and thin rectangular shape, the Duo’s short, squat, and decidedly novel nature was somewhat off-putting at first.
“Where is all that screen real estate I used to have?” I lamented. “Will this thing even fit comfortably in my pocket?”

As it turns out, it does. Front and back pockets, in fact. Even while wearing a case. You can sit down with it in your back pocket, effectively squashing it, and it does not break. (I meant to be more careful, but I forgot to be, repeatedly, as I tend to carry phones in my back pocket when walking around. I sat on the phone countless times. It’s clearly not that fragile.)

I also dropped the phone (by accident!) at least three times. Twice from about table height and once when it got pushed off the side of the bed. It did not fall on soft carpet, but rather on concrete, tile, and wood floors. It didn’t break then either, and the screen didn’t crack. I wouldn’t call these professional drop tests by any means, but it certainly was a relief for someone fairly clumsy with their phone.

Of course, I did encounter some frustrations. I had to scroll more to read back through text threads because of the Duo’s small outer screen; unoptimized apps with numerous controls sometimes had key features tucked away in a “more” (three-dot) menu, leading to a hunt to find the option you needed; and, on multiple occasions, the Google Search app just froze.

Though not Apple’s fault, the latter turned out to be my biggest annoyance software-wise, given that Search is one of my go-to apps especially when traveling. On vacation, I open the app repeatedly to look up points of interest, restaurant reviews, distances between towns, weather, and more. But Google’s app would just stop working, and tapping its back button did nothing.

This seemed to be a problem specific to the Search app’s AI Mode, which these days you’re often dropped into without actually requesting it. (Even more reason to be annoyed by AI Search!) The workaround has been to force-close the app, so the next time you open it, your returned to the home screen with the search box. (It amazes me that, in a time when Google is facing a search decline because of AI, it wouldn’t have prioritized making its Search app functional on Apple’s latest device!)

In addition, many of the early reviews pointed out how many apps were not updated or redesigned for Duo at launch, which meant they had a telltale black bar on the side, cramping the limited screen real estate when the phone is closed even further. This is true, but personally speaking, I didn’t think it was a dealbreaker for making a switch to the Duo.

For one thing, companies have been pushing out their Duo-optimized updates fairly quickly. Those that have not – and there are still more than a few! – continue to be usable. They’re just kind of … ugly.

Google Maps was not Duo-optimized during the trip, yet I had no problem using it for driving directions, local search and discovery, route planning, and the like. If anything, the black-barred apps felt more like an aesthetic issue than a functional problem, even though they’re smaller than usual when the Duo is folded.

I expect all the major apps will eventually update. As for the older apps that never do? Well, it’s probably time to move on from apps no longer being maintained, I’d say, particularly in an era when older software is being exploited left and right by AI-enabled hacking tools.
However, I will agree with the other reviewers who complained about the lack of Face ID.
This is the Duo’s biggest drawback – not the screen, not the camera, not the lack of an Action button for launching your preferred AI assistant. It’s Touch ID.

It is much easier to look at your phone than to fiddle around with finger presses. While I easily avoided the need to use Touch ID to unlock the device – I am almost always wearing an Apple Watch, which serves as an alternative authentication method – I often stumbled when it came to using apps and Apple Pay.

Tap-and-pay is one of the areas where it’s immediately obvious how much smoother Face ID has made everyday tasks. Returning to Touch ID at the time of payment was cumbersome, given that you’re often holding shopping bags, a purse, and, in my case, a dog leash, in addition to the phone you’re using to pay with.

There’s a certain amount of what I guess I’ll call “muscle memory” that you have to overcome when you switch back to Touch ID. I found the easiest grip was to cradle the phone in your hand and use your thumb to authenticate. But where I repeatedly messed up was remembering to keep my thumb or finger on the Touch ID sensor long enough to authenticate. At times, my finger wasn’t situated quite right (I blame the dog pulling on the leash!), and I had to readjust. “I miss Face ID!,” I complained multiple times at checkout.

Though returning to Touch ID was something I got used to, it’s far from ideal. I can see this as being a real stopping point for some early adopters who would otherwise want to move to the Duo. It’s not an insurmountable problem, but it’s among the top reasons not to get the Duo now, in my opinion. (A future version is said to support Face ID.)

Another reason to be wary of the Duo? The camera. Much has been said about the Duo’s lesser camera system. The Duo has two rear cameras to my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s three. It has no telephoto lens. It has a 10x digital zoom versus the Pro’s 40x. The Pro has more advanced hardware for low-light photography and supports ProRAW, ProRes, and other advanced features.
Very simply put: if you are an iPhone photographer or a content creator, you shouldn’t consider the Duo as your primary device.

For, you know, us normal folks, the Duo’s camera is okay. Not great, but fine. What were you going to do with those photos you’re snapping anyway? Post them to Instagram Stories or Facebook? Text them to a friend? Look back on them fondly when they reappear in your photo widget on your Home Screen? Turn them into a Lock Screen wallpaper? None of these things requires a Pro-level camera.

Below are a few photos shot with the Duo versus others shot with the 17 Pro Max. None of the photos are using any special settings or filters; they are intentionally just average, non-professional point-and-shoot shots. Among my complaints are that the Duo’s image processing can, at times, make fine details, like the leaves on trees, look overprocessed. Meanwhile, distant landscapes can appear flatter or smoothed over — though, to be fair, the Blue Ridge Mountains are naturally hazy, so it’s hard to say how much of that is the camera. (Shots from the mountaintop were in low-light conditions — it was getting dark out.)
DUO PHOTOS:
PRO MAX PHOTOS:

As for why to get the phone? This one’s easy; it’s a foldable. From Apple. First, foldables are whimsical in a way that slab phones will never be. They are toys for grown-ups! Developers are also clearly having fun building for the new format, so there are lots of new apps to play with. Plus, it’s a great way to watch movies, particularly with that Duo Folio case with a kickstand.

Second, it’s a foldable from Apple. The company has taken its time to get it right, which comes through in the details, from the barely visible crease to the consistent aspect ratio between screens, allowing content to scale proportionally. It’s also a foldable in Apple’s software ecosystem, which matters for those who move between Apple devices and services and who use and pay for apps that are designed for iOS specifically.
But here’s a small confession: in day-to-day life, I didn’t unfold the Duo as much as I thought I would. (To be clear: I absolutely did unfold it! I just thought I would do it more!)

There are two reasons for this. One: unfolding the device in public invites conversation, and it feels sort of like a flex; I’m not always in a place where I have time to chat. I expect this problem to diminish in time as the novelty wears off.

That said, I still had roughly half a dozen conversations with strangers while I was on vacation, from fellow shoppers to servers to business owners. I even handed them the device at times (when they couldn’t easily run off with it!) and let them fold and unfold it. One person wanted to see the Kid Cue feature in particular, which displays playful Snoopy animations on the phone’s outer display to get children to look toward the camera when you take their picture. They were genuinely delighted by this.

Anecdotally, the consensus was that the unfolded screen was something of a marvel to most: “You can’t see the hinge!” “Is that a screen protector or is it just like that?” (The inner screen has a matte, nano-texture finish, reducing glare. Once explained, it was also praised as “pretty cool.” )

“What if you get sand in it?,” a former Samsung Galaxy Fold owner asked. Their older Android foldable had been ruined after a trip to the beach where sand got into the hinge, causing damage to the screen. (This was not uncommon at the time.) The Duo is rated IP68, the “6” signifying higher dust resistance, making it dust-tight. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 was rated IP48, by comparison. I’m not expecting it will have the same issues, though I do hope a reviewer takes it to the beach soon!

I am certain that at least one of the handful of strangers I spoke to had never actually seen a phone that folded before. The fact that Apple has now made one means this concept will no longer be niche; it will be known to the mainstream.

The other reason I didn’t unfold it as much as I thought is that doing so feels like the start of a more intentional screen time session. When I do unfold the phone now, it’s because I’m truly engaging with what I’m doing on the phone, like watching a show on Netflix or dragging two apps side-by-side in split-screen mode for multitasking. (I love reading news in Inoreader and having X open off to the side to see what people are saying about the news, but that’s a use case that won’t apply to everyone!)

The split-screen feature is easy to use, too – with the app open, you swipe up from the bottom, then drag it to the left or right edge. Target boxes on each side help you visualize where it can move to, which is helpful. (You can also long-press on an app icon to open a split view, but I don’t do this as much.)
But as something of a “mini” phone in terms of screen size when closed, I’m somehow less drawn to what I think of as time-wasting apps like TikTok, Instagram, or casual games.

I’ve been thinking about this, and I don’t believe it’s just the lack of screen real estate when the phone is folded, or the fact that vertical apps haven’t been designed for the Duo’s unfolded landscape screen. Those concerns make sense from a practical, usability standpoint, of course, but there’s something more to this behavioral change, I believe.

For years, phones have been getting bigger, taller, thinner, and more comfortable to hold. Consequently, they easily sucked us into their digital worlds. With the Duo, the design seems to interrupt the way smartphones effortlessly pull us in, begging us to open apps and scroll endlessly.

Rather, the Duo feels like a device you open and use when you have reason to do so, not something you reflexively turn to when you’re bored or have a few minutes to spare. Because the best app use cases are when the phone is unfolded, and unfolding is something you do with careful consideration (and careful hands!), device use becomes more thoughtful.
This is not a bad thing. It also aligns with the embrace of retro tech already underway, where knobs and dials and buttons make engaging with technology feel more deliberate.
And for that reason, despite its faults, the Duo won me over. It’s a phone that’s compelling and fun — a phone I enjoyed picking up, but also found easier to put down.

articles.headline: I shot the same scenes with a pro Viltrox prime lens and a DSLR icon — can you spot the difference?
keyFacts: A TechRadar reviewer tested the new Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens against a 15-year-old Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art lens.
The author reported that the Viltrox lens is slightly sharper at f/1.4 and handles chromatic aberration better, though differences level out at smaller apertures.
The reviewer concluded that older DSLR optics like the Sigma remain a viable option today and plans to keep using it.
body: If I was to pinpoint one special lens in my photography career, it would have to be the Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art for Nikon F-mount.

I picked mine up just before I moved to East Africa where I would work in photo journalism. Sigma had just burst onto the scene with its new ‘Art’ lens in 2012, for a much lower price than Nikon’s proprietary 35mm f/1.4 for its DSLRs, and so I bought one to pair with my Nikon D800 camera.

Over four memorable years living in Kenya and travelling the region and neighbouring countries, I estimate that I took more than 75% of my photos with this one lens, many my all-time favorites of people in their environment.
More recently, I switched to a mirrorless camera made by the same company — the Z-mount Nikon Z6 II, which has been updated with the Z6 III but remains my primary camera.

Viltrox then offered a review sample of its shiny new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens, which was unveiled this week in Nikon Z-mount and Sony E-mount versions, but with no word on an L-mount version yet. I’ve already tested Viltrox’s pricier 35mm F1.2 from its flagship ‘Lab’ series, but the latest f/1.4 pro is a specs match to my old lens, so I was keen to see how the two compared.
I tried both lenses in various scenarios, shooting like-for-like photos with them using the Z6 II camera (the Sigma lens attached via the Nikon F-mount to Z-mount adapter).
Along the way I was asking myself — is mirrorless all that it’s cracked up to be, or could I happily continue with my decade-old-and-more DSLR optic? Here’s what I learned.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Handling of each lens
I'll start with handling, and Sigma’s lens by itself is physically smaller than Viltrox’s. However, the necessary F-mount to Z-mount adapter to use it with my Z6 II adds bulk and evens matters out.

And if I were to use the Sigma lens with my D800 DSLR, well, that's a much bigger camera than the Z6 II. The adapter essentially addresses flange depth (the distance between the camera sensor and the rear of the lens — which is deeper in Nikon's F-mount), while maintaining full autofocus performance.

As such, there was no real size or weight advantage to either lens, whatever camera system was used. Nikon also has an affordable 35mm f/1.4 Z-mount lens, mind you, which is smaller than both of these lenses, but in my experience it doesn't match the quality of either lens here.

My Sigma lens has taken a beating over its almost 15 years of use in harsh conditions, and it's still going strong. Sure, it looks well-used, but it performs like it did on day one. I wouldn't hold the same hope for the Viltrox lens, aesthetically speaking, at least. It's one of the many Viltrox lenses that I've tested with an exterior that scratches easily. That doesn't affect optical quality, but it did make me mindful of taking care of the lens.

Autofocus is a fraction snappier and smoother with the Viltrox lens, but not enough of a reason alone to opt for it. I don't believe that using an F-mount lens through the adapter with a Z-mount mirrorless camera has any adverse affect on autofocus performance.
Optical quality: any obvious progress?

I regularly want to make use of the bright maximum f/1.4 aperture with a lens such as these, in order to decrease depth of field and blur surroundings so that my subjects standout, and for working in dim light with no supplementary lighting. It’s at this setting in particular that the differences in optical quality between the two lenses are acute.

The Viltrox lens is optically sharper at f/1.4. Not by much, I must say, and you won't necessarily see the difference even when viewed on a laptop — I'd still class the Sigma lens as very sharp. However, when pixel peeping, the difference is there.

And it's when pixel peeping that chromatic aberration (CA) in the Sigma is way more pronounced. The Viltrox lens isn't immune to it, but it handles the distortion much better. The Sigma lens shows longitudinal chromatic aberration (LoCA) at times, too — a lens distortion that is harder to correct. I expected vignetting (where corners are darker) to be worse in the Sigma lens, but in reality performance was roughly on par.
- Check out my round-up of the best Nikon Z-mount lenses

And what about bokeh (the out-of-focus quality, typically observed in dappled light)? From my sample images, I'd have to say it's a tie. Both lenses can render buttery smooth bokeh, with similar characteristics; roundish in the center of the frame, becoming slightly more cats-eye in shape towards the corners.

The optical quality observations above are made with the lens aperture wide open at f/1.4. In all the situations above, I took sequences at f/1.4, f/1.8, f/2, f/2.8, f/4 and f/5.6 and compared the differences.

Stop aperture down to, say, f/4 and f/5.6, and most of the above differences are negligible; sharpness evens out, and lens distortions reduce — only does chromatic aberration remain more pronounced in the Sigma. I've included closeups of images shot at f/5.6 which prove how the quality evens out, below.
Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro vs Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art: the bottom line
For photographers, there is surprisingly little to choose between what is an excellent Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens and the 15-year-old Sigma 35mm f/1.4 DG HSM Art.

Optical quality differences are more acute at f/1.4; with aperture at its maximum setting, the Viltrox lens is slightly sharper and handles chromatic aberration better. However, you'll only really spot those differences when pixel peeping, and closing down each lens to f/4 and lower, the end results level out.
Bokeh is essentially the same in both lenses, although there's a touch of LoCA in the Sigma lens in certain backlit scenarios.

The Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro joins a growing list of lenses from the Chinese company that I can highly recommend. However, comparing it to a 15-year-old Sigma legend, that's designed for a mostly discontinued camera system, has only shown me that DSLRs and their best optics are still a decent option today. I for one will happily continue using my Sigma lens for photography.

Tim joined the TechRadar team as Cameras Editor in 2023 and has enjoyed more than 15 years as a tech journalist specializing in camera gear. He's previously worked at Amateur Photographer, for a photo accessory manufacturer and as a freelance photographer and video producer, with clients including Studio 44 and Canon. He also started a media team in Nairobi, Kenya, where he lived for a few years volunteering for a faith-based organisation. Tim is married, father of three children, and loves being active, primarily running since hanging up his football boots.

articles.headline: CodePink leader adds muscle to well-funded fight to ban restaurant delicacy
keyFacts: District of Columbia residents are voting on a local ballot measure called Initiative 86 to ban foie gras and other products made from birds.
Financial records show the campaign has collected nearly half a million dollars, with the Portland-based nonprofit Pro-Animal Future providing the majority of the funding.
Critics and local restaurant owners raised concerns that the measure's wording could accidentally ban common poultry products and lead to further restrictions on meat.
body: WASHINGTON, D.C. — CodePink D.C. Coordinator Olivia DiNucci last month posted a TikTok video of herself in a home supporting an issue far afield from her usual battles supporting the Communist Party of Cuba and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

This time, she was backing a local ballot measure, "Initiative 86," introduced in early February in the D.C. City Council to ban foie gras, a fine-dining delicacy made from duck liver, and other products made from birds. D.C. residents will vote on the measure on election day with early voting already started.

The campaign presents itself as a grassroots effort to advance animal welfare, but public financial filings reveal a far more heavily funded operation. A national animal-rights network has supplied hundreds of thousands of dollars in financial support, underwriting paid petition circulators, political consultants, staff salaries and advertising in a campaign that could reshape Washington’s restaurant industry. Far from a shoestring local initiative, the effort has reported nearly half a million dollars in contributions and expenditures, much of it backed by an organization that openly describes local ballot measures as stepping stones toward a broader "pro-animal future."
WHO’S FUNDING AMERICA’S PROTEST UNREST? FOX NATION'S NEW 'RIOT INC.' FOLLOWS THE MONEY TO FIND OUT

A Fox News Digital investigation of campaign-finance records, nonprofit filings and the groups’ own organizing documents traces the people, money and long-term strategy behind Initiative 86 and raises questions about how a fight over one luxury menu item became part of a much larger political campaign over what Americans eat.

Pro-Animal Future, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit based in Portland, Ore., launched the campaign, nicknamed I-86, in D.C. and says its local ballot efforts are part of a broader push to change public attitudes toward common animal agricultural practices. Its IRS filing also lists its name as Pro-Animal DC .
In seven financial reports filed with the D.C. Office of Campaign Finance, Pro-Animal DC provides a window into a local political campaign’s operational, financial and logistical infrastructure.

According to its latest filings , Pro-Animal DC collected a whopping $474,190.62 between Sept. 23, 2025, and Oct. 26, 2026, for the local campaign, with Pro-Animal Future as its major backer, providing it $386,435.77.

Its largest expense is stipends totaling $126,780.36, or about one-quarter of the campaign’s expenses, to a paid professional protest organizer: Cady Witt, whose LinkedIn profile lists her as "community impact coordinator" at "DC Voters for Animals." Witt is also listed as the treasurer of Pro-Animal DC in its campaign reports.

Pro-Animal DC reported another $89,224.00, or about 20% of its expenses, for 293 payments to 64 people described as "consultant - circulator" from September 2025 through October 26, 2026. They got an average payment of $1,394.13 per person.
‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA

Also a professional organizer, CodePink’s DiNucci is typically a fixture at anti-Israel demonstrations and foreign affairs hearings. CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans is married to an American-born, China-based tech tycoon, Neville Roy Singham , whose funding of activist groups has drawn scrutiny from congressional lawmakers and is the subject of a federal investigation. Pro Animal Future said CodePink doesn’t have a role in its campaign beyond DiNucci’s appearance in her TikTok video.

Pro-Animal Future alleges that birds are "force fed" to gain the weight needed to produce foie gras, and it says its campaigns seek to end "force-feeding" birds and shift public views on animal agriculture. According to its latest available IRS 990 tax filing, Pax Fauna, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Denver, says it’s related to Pro-Animal Future, which it described as doing "lobbying" work.
In 2024, Pax Fauna outlined a 10-year roadmap to build local ballot campaigns and eventually pursue statewide " factory-farming" bans and establish "animal freedom."

The roadmap called such measures a way to "provoke a sort of identity crisis for the voting public" and "storm the nation". The group sought to launch as many as 10 local chapters during the 2025-2026 election cycle.

An anonymous purchaser bought the web domain ProAnimalDC.org in April 2025, according to online records . Today, Pro-Animal Future lists its current campaigns as running in D.C. and Denver and says it worked with Portland’s City Council to ban foie gras sales this past June.
Pax Fauna’s founders said they have spent years organizing with Direct Action Everywhere, an animal-rights 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Berkeley, Ca.

Last year, according to its filings , Pro-Animal Future spent $7,703.70 for Airbnb accommodations. This year, on July 31, it spent $22,418.69 for Airbnb accommodations. Pro-Animal DC has stated that the lodging was for about 60 out-of-town "volunteers" who came to Washington, D.C., in July for a signature-gathering effort called "Goosapalooza." On its website , it promoted the "free housing."

The measure’s language has raised questions about how far the ban could reach. Its definition of a "fattened bird liver product" covers food or byproducts made from birds’ livers when the birds were fattened "through any method or practice," and specifically lists pâtés, spreads and processed meat products as products to be banned. The initiative separately defines "force-feeding" as causing a bird to eat more than it would voluntarily consume.
MAMDANI ACCUSED OF BETRAYING NYC WORKERS AS UNION BOSS BLASTS 'ANTI-LABOR' HORSE CARRIAGE BAN
Former D.C. Attorney General Karl Racine told City Cast DC, a local media outlet, that the text "includes le poulet," which means chicken in French.
Jon Mandel, an attorney and former D.C. Council legislative staffer, told the same outlet, that the sales provision could reach poultry-liver products made without force-feeding.

Pro-Animal Future spokeswoman Natalie Fulton told City Cast DC the campaign isn’t trying to ban chicken and "is about foie gras." She added that the D.C. Council could clarify the language if voters approve the measure.

However, restaurants in the district who serve the delicacy aren't buying what activists are selling. Bart Hutchins, chef and co-owner of Butterworth’s, a Capitol Hill restaurant popular with Trump administration members, raised a similar concern in an interview with Fox News Digital. "Realistically that could ban at least 20 products that I can think of right off the top of my head that aren’t foie gras," he said. Hutchins said his restaurant would consider legal challenges if the measure passes.

Hutchins sees the initiative as part of a broader effort to restrict what Americans can eat. "If they ban foie gras here, they’ll eventually ban meat here, and they’ll bring that to the rest of the country," he said.
Pro-Animal Future’s 10-year roadmap calls for statewide factory-farming bans but doesn’t define "factory farming." Hutchins said he worries the term could be interpreted broadly.

This week, the dispute followed Hutchins to the 17th Street NW "High Heel Race," a Halloween drag event in the District. Witt, D.C. campaign director for Pro-Animal Future, appeared dressed as Hutchins, wearing a chef’s hat, glasses, a drawn-on mustache and a white corseted outfit.

Nearby, a person in a duck costume crouched with a feeding tube in its mouth. Washingtonian food editor Jessica Sidman shared photos on X, describing Witt simply as "Pro-Animal campaign coordinator." By late Thursday, the photos had 42,200 views, amplifying the campaign even further. Hutchins didn't appear phased by the mimicking, he took to X and said, "Bart derangement syndrome enters the lexicon."

The measure has also drawn opposition from celebrity chef José Andrés, whose D.C. restaurant serves foie gras. He questioned the ban’s broader implications on X, asking, "If duck goes, all goes next?"

The D.C. chief financial officer, Glen Lee, estimates implementing the measure would cost $314,000 from fiscal 2026 through 2029, including $274,000 for an additional inspector and $40,000 for public education. The fiscal impact statement says the District’s Department of Energy and Environment doesn’t inspect restaurant kitchens or other back-of-house operations and isn’t likely to do so. It says the inspector would investigate complaints, inspect establishments and coordinate with other agencies, but doesn’t detail how regulators would verify a product’s origin during routine inspections.

Hutchins said he would continue serving foie gras until the city resolves how to enforce the measure. He disputes the animal-welfare case for a ban, saying he doesn’t believe the feeding process that farms use to create foie gras hurts ducks. Pro-Animal DC’s findings say the practice causes pain and illness. Hutchins also said losing D.C. as a major market could threaten the country’s two commercial foie gras producers, Hudson Valley Foie Gras and La Belle Farm in New York state’s Catskills region.

The measure would regulate sales in D.C. The D.C. chief financial officer’s fiscal impact statement says, "The Office of Revenue Analysis is not aware of any bird farms or bird feeding operations in the District."

The Catskill Foie Gras Collective, a producer group, says its member farms raise ducks cage-free and use small, flexible plastic tubes to deliver feed to a pouch in their throats. It argues the process causes no pain, citing ducks’ anatomy, and says feeding is skipped if a bird hasn't finished digesting its previous meal. The collective also says Catskills foie gras farms employ about 400 people.
GET BREAKING NEWS ALERTS

Fox News Digital reached out to Pro-Animal DC, which disputed critics’ claim that Initiative 86’s wording could extend to poultry-liver products beyond foie gras. The campaign said the measure is intended only to prohibit force-feeding and foie gras sales. It said "fattened" refers to the extreme enlargement of birds’ livers associated with foie gras production, not ordinary poultry farming. The campaign pointed to the measure’s findings, which describe covered products as luxury foods made from diseased, enlarged livers, and said the broad definition of "bird" is meant to prevent producers from switching species.
SEND US A TIP

Pro-Animal DC said D.C. agencies and courts look to a law’s stated purpose when its wording allows more than one interpretation, and said it would welcome Council clarification if voters approve the measure. Asked what language could clarify the measure, spokeswoman Natalie Fulton didn’t elaborate.

The dispute leaves D.C. voters weighing a ballot measure presented as a foie gras ban while others raise broader questions about its wording, enforcement and the campaign’s long-term goals. For Hutchins, the stakes extend beyond one item on a restaurant menu; for Pro-Animal Future, Initiative 86 is one step in a larger effort to change farming practices at a national scale.
Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani and Ava Palschakov contributed to this report.

articles.headline: Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update
keyFacts: Konami released patch 1.6.0 for Silent Hill: Townfall on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store.
The update adds a new Hard difficulty mode, rebalances existing settings, and adjusts resources and enemy hearing.
Players also received user interface improvements, bug fixes, and a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option on PC.
body: Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.
Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.
SILENT HILL: Townfall
Notice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)
An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.
Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.
*The PlayStation®5 version is…
— Silent Hill Official (@SilentHill) October 29, 2026

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.
PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.
To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.
Below are the full patch notes:
PlayStation 5 / Steam / Epic Games Store
Gameplay
- Addition of a new Hard difficulty mode
- Rebalance of gameplay elements across all difficulty modes to accommodate the introduction of the new Hard mode, creating a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from.
- Resource adjustment in some sections of the game as part of difficulty balancing.
- Player position now visible on the map in all difficulty modes.
- Enemy hearing sensitivity now varies by difficulty, increasing with the difficulty level.
- The Weight’s attack severity reduction is limited to Story Mode only.
UX / UI
- Nightmare difficulty warning screen now shown if first playthrough is set to Nightmare difficulty.
- Difficulty selection description now shows a clearer summary of differences between the options.
- Improvements to valve status lighting for colourblind players.
- Additional player hints / tutorials added.
- Improvements to some puzzle hints and item wording.
- Restructuring of the Options Menu to better separate options into categories.
- Renamed the controls remapping menu option so that it does not explicitly mention only control pads, as keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too.
Other
- DLSS Ray Reconstruction option added (PC only).
- General improvements and bug fixes.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. articles.headline: Carragher apologises to Villa for 'wrong' language
keyFacts: Jamie Carragher apologised to Aston Villa, their owners, and fans for using clumsy and wrong language about manager Unai Emery.
Aston Villa stated they would initiate legal action against Carragher for unacceptable insults after he claimed Emery would want to manage Manchester United.
Carragher explained on social media that his podcast comments, which included telling Villa fans to shut up, were intended as a joke.
body: - Published
Jamie Carragher has apologised to Aston Villa, the club's owners and their fans for using "clumsy and wrong" language when linking manager Unai Emery with becoming Manchester United head coach.
On Friday, Villa said they would initiate legal action against the former England defender for what they described as "unacceptable insults".
The club's statement, signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris, referred to comments made by Carragher on the Stick to Football podcast, when he suggested Emery would want to manage a "giant" club.
He also told the club's fans to shut up, adding: "Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."
Posting on social media on Saturday, Carragher said his comments were intended to be "tongue in cheek".
"I'd like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners and their fans," the pundit wrote.
"My language this week was clumsy and wrong.
"I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it's not come across that way, so apologies."
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick's position is hanging in the balance following a dismal start to the season.
Referring to former Paris St-Germain and Arsenal boss Emery, Carragher said on Stick to Football: "Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again.
"There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.

"So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."

After his comments attracted criticism from Villa fans, Carragher responded on social media, stating that telling them to shut up had been "a joke" and he had been praising Emery and the club "for years".

He reiterated on the Overlap Daily podcast that his message to Villa fans had been meant "in jest", adding: "I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking, what's the best we can get?"

articles.headline: Lefty late-night TV hosts targeted Republicans in 87% of jokes about Senate candidates: study
keyFacts: A study by the Media Research Center found that 87% of late-night TV jokes about U.S. Senate candidates targeted Republicans.
The analysis showed that only seven jokes knocked a Democrat, while Republican candidates like Ken Paxton and Susan Collins received significantly more attention.
MRC President David Bozell stated that late-night comedy has become predictable and that comedy is sharpest when nobody is off limits.
body: Late-night television continues to be as lefty as ever — with 87% of jokes targeting U.S. Senate candidates directed at Republicans, a new analysis found.
Only seven jokes knocked a Democrat, according to a Media Research Center study provided exclusively to The Post.

Fourteen wisecracks were aimed at Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic state Representative James Talarico for the US Senate; nine slammed Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is trying to fend off Democratic challenger Troy Jackson; and six targeted Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, who is running for an open seat against far-left Dem Abdul El-Sayed.

“This guy is awful,” goofed comedian Michael Kosta about Paxton on the Sept. 10 airing for “The Daily Show.” “Are they really running this charisma black-hole in one of the most important Senate races in the country?”
The study did not include tracking gags against other pols, including President Donald Trump, who continues to be the butt of the late-night TV’s jokes.

The Post previoulsy reported on another Media Research Center report that found 92% of late-night TV jokes targeted the right in 2025 – with a jaw-dropping 7,045 of them slamming Trump. In 2024, late-night comedians targeted Trump 5,980 times.

Reps for “The Daily Show,” “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” “The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon” and “Late Night with Seth Meyers” did not return messages.
